passage:
"Just say it, Indu," Payal whispered at the lunch benches. "Say Rani smells funny."
"But she doesn't."
"Then you can sit somewhere else."
Indu's hands went cold. She laughed a small laugh that she did not mean, and Rani looked at her food.
"That was not funny," Indu said later, at the tap. "I'm sorry, Rani."
"Why did you do it?"
"I was scared they'd throw me out."
Next day Payal handed her a note to pass around. Indu quietly put it back in Payal's bag and said, "I'm not doing this one." Two girls, Meena and Sonal, shrugged and sat down next to her.

qa.q: Who did Payal want Indu to say smelled funny?
qa.a: Payal wanted Indu to say that Rani smells funny.

qa.q: Why did Indu laugh at first even though she did not mean it?
qa.a: She was scared of being thrown out of the group, so she went along with the mean joke.

qa.q: What small step did Indu take that showed who her real friends were?
qa.a: She refused just one thing, passing the note, and saw that Meena and Sonal still sat down with her.

qa.q: What might Rani have felt when Indu apologised at the tap?
qa.a: Rani may have felt hurt but also a little relieved that Indu admitted she was wrong, though she asked why it happened.

grounding: A child goes along with mean things out of fear of being expelled, then quietly refuses one thing and sees who stands by her.

passage:
Wednesday night
Jomon's diary. Today Kalyani told us all to stop talking to Sajan because he 'acts weird'. I didn't even argue. I just turned my back on him at the bus stop like everyone else, and I felt disgusting the whole ride. Last week I laughed when they hid his water bottle. I only do it because I'm scared they'll kick me out and I'll be alone. But then I'm the kind of person who hides water bottles. Tomorrow I'm going to try one small thing: I'll say hi to Sajan. Just hi. No speech. Then I'll see who's still sitting with me at lunch. And if they keep picking on him, I'm telling Ma'am. If nobody sits with me after that, at least I'll know what that group really was.

qa.q: What did the group hide last week?
Why did Jomon go along with ignoring Sajan?
qa.a: Out of fear of being kicked out and left alone, even though it made Jomon feel disgusting.

qa.q: What small step does Jomon plan?
qa.a: To quietly say hi to Sajan without a speech, see who still sits at lunch, and tell the teacher if the picking-on continues.

qa.q: What might Sajan be going through?
qa.a: He is probably confused and lonely, with people turning their backs on him and hiding his things.

grounding: A child writes about joining in with meanness out of fear of losing the group, and plans one quiet refusal.

passage: In the village school near Jorhat, the girls under the peepal tree had a game: whenever Bhupen walked past in his patched shirt, they sang, 'Here comes the scarecrow.' Urmila always sang too, softer than the others. She hated it. But Minoti, who led the group, had once dropped a girl just for not laughing, and nobody sat with that girl for a month. On Monday Bhupen walked past again. The song started. Urmila kept her mouth shut and looked down at her slate. Minoti noticed. 'What's wrong with you?' 'Nothing. I just don't want to.' Minoti sniffed and turned away. Three girls followed her. But Juri stayed, and quietly slid closer to Urmila on the tree root.

qa.q: What did the group sing when Bhupen walked past?
Why had Urmila always sung, even though she hated it?
qa.a: She was afraid of being dropped, like the girl nobody sat with for a month.

qa.q: What did Urmila's quiet refusal show her?
qa.a: Who truly stood by her: three girls followed Minoti, but Juri stayed beside her.

qa.q: How might Bhupen feel hearing the song every day?
qa.a: Humiliated and hurt about his patched shirt, and perhaps relieved to notice one voice go quiet.

grounding: A village girl who went along with mocking out of fear quietly refuses once and sees who still stands by her.
